html:
Olive oil and wine were the great trade goods of the ancient Greek world, carried by sea in clay jars called amphoras. By the 3rd century BCE this trade linked the whole Mediterranean and the Black Sea.

An amphora was a tall jar with two handles and a pointed foot, which let it be packed tightly in a ship's hold and tied in place. Greek cities stamped the handles with marks naming a maker or an official of the year. Archaeologists use these stamps to date the jars and trace where they went. Rhodes and Knidos were big wine exporters in this period, and wines from islands such as Chios and Thasos were prized. Athens had long been known for its olive oil, which filled the prize jars of the Panathenaic Games.

Wrecks show the trade at work. The Kyrenia ship, which sank off Cyprus around 300 BCE, was carrying hundreds of amphoras. Wine was drunk mixed with water at the symposium, and cities grew rich on the trade, such as Rhodes and later Delos. Rome continued it on a vast scale; Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill of broken oil jars.
sum: Olive oil and wine were the great trade goods of the ancient Greek world, carried by sea in clay jars called amphoras. By the 3rd century BCE this trade linked the whole Mediterranean and the Black Sea.
